memoryText: You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Leviticus 19:2 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Leviticus 19:2 is the call that sums up the whole book. It is spoken to “all the congregation of the people of Israel,” not just to the priests. Holiness is the vocation of every member of God’s people.

“You shall be holy.” The word means set apart, belonging to God. It has two sides. It means separation from what is sinful and common, and it means dedication to God. A holy person is not simply someone who avoids certain things. He is someone who belongs to God.

“For I the LORD your God am holy.” This is the reason, and it is the whole reason. The command is not based on a rule but on a person. Israel is to be holy because their God is holy. The people of a holy God are to resemble him, as children resemble a father.

Notice the next verses in chapter 19. Holiness is not only about worship. It is about respect for parents, care for the poor, honesty in business, and love for your neighbor. To be holy is to reflect God’s character in ordinary life.

For the Christian, Peter quotes the verse: “As he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, You shall be holy, for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:15-16). The call is the same, but the power is greater. In Christ you have been made holy, and the Holy Spirit lives in you to make you so.
weekInReview: This week you studied the heart of the book of Leviticus. You read about clean and unclean animals and the laws of skin disease, and you saw how the priest goes outside the camp to welcome a healed person back. You read the Day of Atonement, with the high priest entering the Most Holy Place and the two goats, one sacrificed and one sent away. You prayed Psalm 51, the prayer of a broken and contrite heart. You read the unit’s anchor verse, Leviticus 17:11, about the life in the blood. You read the Holiness Code, with the great command to love your neighbor as yourself, and the laws for priests and offerings. The week taught that atonement is costly and given by God, and that a forgiven people are called to be holy.
reflectionQuestions: The Day of Atonement showed sin being paid for and carried away. Which of these two pictures, the sacrificed goat or the scapegoat, speaks to you most today? Why?

Hebrews says that Jesus is both the high priest who enters the Most Holy Place and the sacrifice whose blood is offered. How does it change your sense of security to know that your priest and your sacrifice are the same person?
Leviticus 19 ties holiness to ordinary things like honest scales and care for the poor. Where in your daily life is God calling you to reflect his holiness more clearly?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that in Christ you have been set apart.
Ask him to help you love your neighbor as yourself this week.
Rest in his finished work today.
